Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning

Hugo Cui Affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Laboratoire de mathématiques d’Orsay, 91405, Orsay, France    Francesca Mignacco Affiliation: Joseph Henry Laboratories of Physics and Lewis–Sigler Institute, Princeton University, Princeton NJ 08544, USA Affiliation: Initiative for the Theoretical Sciences, The Graduate Center, City University of New York, 365 Fifth Ave, New York NY 10016, USA    Francesco Mori Affiliation: Center of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Harvard University, 20 Garden Street, Cambridge MA 02138, USA
Abstract

We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost Δ\Delta. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.

Introduction

Many breakthroughs in modern deep learning were achieved by training models on ever-accruing volumes of data. Yet, there exist important domains of application where labeled data is scarce. Examples include medical diagnosis (Liu, 2004), rare languages (Kholodna et al., 2024) or molecular modeling (Felis and Dononelli, 2025), where data annotation requires either a human expert, or expensive ab-initio simulations, resulting in prohibitive labeling costs. In such scenarios, it is thus essential to carefully select which samples, among a stream of unlabeled data, should be labeled.

In the present manuscript, we consider the online setting, where unlabeled data points are viewed sequentially. For each sample, the model can decide either to output a prediction, and incur a cost in case of mistake, or to query the label from a (e.g., human) expert, paying the associated annotation cost, and use the thus labeled instance to perform a gradient step, furthering its training. For example, in medical applications, a diagnosis must be issued by the model to every patient, unless it is determined further examinations need to be performed first by an expert. Querying such additional examinations is however typically costly, and thus must be done sparingly. If performed however, such examinations provide an additional data point that can improve the model accuracy, thereby reducing the frequency of future expert queries. How then to choose which labels to query, and when?

Many selection policies were proposed in the literature on online active learning (Dasgupta et al., 2005; Hanneke, 2014) and selective sampling (Réveillard et al., 2025; Hanneke and Yang, 2021; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2009), some of which were shown to achieve the optimal rates of mistakes, queries or accuracy. These works, however, typically fix the form of the query policy in advance and analyze its performance. Here, we take a complementary approach and ask what the optimal policy schedule is. We consider the classical problem of online binary linear classification in the realizable case with the Adatron learning rule (Anlauf and Biehl, 1989; Motzkin and Schoenberg, 1954), under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional limit where the dimension dd of the samples is comparable to the total number nn of unlabeled data (Seung et al., 1992a; Kinzel and Rujan, 1990; Watkin and Rau, 1992; Engel and van den Broeck, 2001; Rattray and Saad, 1997). Using techniques from statistical physics and control theory, we precisely ascertain the optimal query policy schedule among a class of margin-based policies that minimizes, down to the constant, a given cost objective — either the generalization error under a labeling budget, or the cumulative number of mistakes and queries.

More precisely, we distinguish between myopic policies, which greedily minimize at all times the instantaneous increment in the objective, and horizon-optimized schedules, obtained by numerically optimizing the selection policies across all training times to minimize the objective at the end of training. Two classes of margin-based policies will prove of particular interest: inner-margin policies, which query only samples within a threshold distance of the decision boundary, and intermediate-margin policies, which query samples whose distance lies between two thresholds, thus discarding both the closest and the farthest samples. Our main contributions are:

  • •

    We first study policies that minimize the generalization error given nn unlabeled samples, under a total query budget γ​n\gamma n, with γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1]. We show that the myopic strategy is of the intermediate-margin type. Within this class, we then compute the horizon-optimized threshold schedules, which achieve a lower final generalization error than random, myopic, and inner-margin strategies.

  • •

    We then consider the setting where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost Δ>0\Delta>0. We derive an exact expression for the myopic policy, showing that it is an inner-margin rule with shrinking threshold. We propose a simple selection heuristic inspired therefrom, and compare its performance with other baselines on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. In the same setting, the horizon-optimized schedule is again an inner-margin rule, with higher query rate early in training, outperforming both the myopic and the random policies, with gains that grow with Δ\Delta.

  • •

    Finally, we study myopic policies for cumulative-cost minimization in two-layer neural networks, allowing them to take as an argument the full vector of preactivations. We exemplify how inner-margin policies naively applied to the network readout are suboptimal.

The code used in the manuscript can be found in the following repository.

Related works

Stream-based active learning.

A now mature body of works has studied the label complexity of online active learning, ascertaining the minimal number of queries necessary to achieve a given accuracy (Freund and Schapire, 1997; Freund et al., 1997; Hanneke, 2014). The realizable case where the two classes lie in distinct half-spaces, in particular, has been the object of refined analyses. Dasgupta et al. (2005); Yan and Zhang (2017) construct active learning algorithms achieving the optimal O~​(d​log⁡1/ϵ)\tilde{O}(d\log\nicefrac{{1}}{{\epsilon}}) label complexity required to reach accuracy 1−ϵ1-\epsilon. The present work complements these results in the high-dimensional Gaussian setting, and investigates, given a number nn of unlabeled instances and a query budget γ​n\gamma n, the minimal generalization error achievable, down to the constant, within a class of margin-based query policies.

Selective sampling.

In problems where the learner needs to output a prediction after viewing each sample, one aims at minimizing the cumulative number of mistakes over training, rather than the final accuracy (Réveillard et al., 2025; Hanneke and Yang, 2021; Gangrade et al., 2021; Yu and Blanchard, 2026; Goel et al., 2023). Formally, a selective sampling algorithm must determine at each iteration whether to issue a prediction, or instead query the label, with the goal of minimizing the overall number of mistakes and queries. The latter can be controlled for a variety of algorithms, as studied in Réveillard et al. (2025); Hanneke and Yang (2021). Some of these guarantees however become vacuous in high-dimensional settings. In the present work, in the case where mistakes have unit cost and queries have cost Δ\Delta, we precisely characterize the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, and ascertain its large-time asymptotic behavior down to the constant.

Optimal schedules for high-dimensional online learning.

In contrast to most works on online active or selective learning, which offer theoretical guarantees for a specific algorithm, this paper investigates the optimal query strategy. Formally, this amounts to ascertaining the optimal schedule of selection policies, such that the learning process driven thereby realizes minimal cost or error, while respecting a query budget. The large dimensionality d≫1d\gg 1 of the space in which the process is embedded, however, seemingly poses significant barriers to the application of standard control-theoretic approaches. For Gaussian data nevertheless, the training dynamics (including instantaneous accuracy and mistake rates) can be succinctly described by a finite set of scalar ordinary differential equations (ODEs) (Saad and Solla, 1995a; Saad and Solla, 1995b; Biehl and Schwarze, 1995; Goldt et al., 2019; Arous et al., 2021; Collins-Woodfin et al., 2024), on which standard variational and control analyses can be applied. This route allows for a precise characterization of optimal hyperparameter schedules, including learning rate (Rattray and Saad, 1997; Rattray and Saad, 1998; Bordelon and Mori, 2026), task ordering (Mori et al., 2025) or dropout (Mori and Mignacco, 2025; Mignacco and Mori, 2026). A generalization to functional hyperparameter schedules was exposed in Rattray and Saad (1997). We draw from this conceptual framework to find optimal selection policies for active half-space learning in high dimensions.

Active learning half-spaces in high dimensions.

The question of active half-space learning in the proportional high-dimensional regime n≍dn\asymp d has received a long and sustained attention, notably in the pool-based setting (Cui et al., 2021; Kolossov et al., 2023; Dohmatob et al., 2025; Sorscher et al., 2022; Askari-Hemmat et al., 2025; Cui and Lu, 2026), focusing on inner-margin policies. Derényi et al. (1994) study the converse problem where samples farthest from the ground-truth separator are retained, providing a characterization of the optimal threshold. The online setting was first studied by Seung et al. (1992b); Kinzel and Rujan (1990); Watkin and Rau (1992); Zhou (2019), in the case where the learner is allowed to design and synthesize specific samples at each step and query the accompanying label. Kinzel and Rujan (1990); Watkin and Rau (1992) in particular study the prescription of designing samples orthogonal to the running weights, which corresponds to an inner-margin policy with vanishing threshold. Parrondo and van den Broeck (1993) conversely consider the case where large-margin samples are retained, while Jung and Opper (1996) study gradient-based selections. Closer to our work, Mai et al. (2022) derive a sharp characterization of online stream-based active learning with repeated retrainings, and determine the optimal batch size for a two-step procedure. All the above works, however, assume a specific functional form for the selection policy. Here, we derive myopic policies analytically and numerically compute horizon-optimized candidates within the same functional class. While in certain settings these policies indeed correspond to inner-margin policies, as studied in prior works, we find that they can also prescribe the retention of samples at intermediate margins. The present manuscript also offers a precise characterization of the optimal schedule of such selection functions over the course of training.

1 Problem setup

Online active classification.

We consider the problem of active online learning with a linear classifier, under Gaussian design. A stream of nn unlabeled samples (xi)i∈[n](x_{i})_{i\in[n]}, drawn i.i.d from a d−d-dimensional Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(0d,Id/d)\mathcal{N}(0_{d},\nicefrac{{I_{d}}}{{d}}), is sequentially observed by the learner. At each round i∈[n]i\in[n], the learner can

  • •

    Query an expert to annotate the sample, thereby obtaining the associated label yiy_{i}. We consider the realizable setting, where there exists an (unknown) ground truth vector β∈ℝd\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ∥β∥2=d\lVert\beta\rVert^{2}=d that perfectly separates the data, namely yj=sign⁡(⟨β,xj⟩)y_{j}=\mathrm{sign}(\left\langle\beta,x_{j}\right\rangle) for all j∈[n]j\in[n]. With the full covariate-label pair (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) now available, the learner may then perform a gradient update on the weights wiw_{i} of a linear classifier

    wi+1=wi−η​ℓ′​(⟨wi,xi⟩​yi)​yi​xi,\displaystyle w_{i+1}=w_{i}-\eta\ell^{\prime}(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle y_{i})y_{i}x_{i}, (1)

    with learning rate η>0\eta>0 and loss ℓ:ℝ→ℝ+\ell\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+}. Note that this training process corresponds to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) at batch size 11.

  • •

    Alternatively, the learner may choose to not pay the cost of querying an expert, and instead issue a prediction sign(⟨wi,xi⟩)\sgn(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle) for the unknown label yiy_{i} of sample xix_{i}, at the risk of making a mistake whenever sign(⟨wi,xi⟩)≠yi\sgn(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle)\neq y_{i}.

In line with prior works on active binary classification (Engel and van den Broeck, 2001; Dasgupta et al., 2005; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2009; Sculley, 2007), we focus on the 0−0-threshold squared hinge loss ℓ⁡(z)=1/2​min⁡(z,0)2\ell(z)=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\min(z,0)^{2}, for which the gradient update (1) reduces to the celebrated Adatron rule (Anlauf and Biehl, 1989; Motzkin and Schoenberg, 1954). The latter has been repeatedly leveraged in active learning analyses for its favorable convergence properties: in the passive case, the Adatron rule achieves a fast 1/i\nicefrac{{1}}{{i}} decay in generalization error (Engel and van den Broeck, 2001) while in the active setting, it can lead to exponential decay with the number of labeled instances (Dasgupta et al., 2005). For extensions to the logistic loss, see App. E.

Selection policy.

At every round i∈[n]i\in[n], the choice of the learner can be encoded by a binary variable σi∈{0,1}\sigma_{i}\in\{0,1\}, with the learner choosing to query the label (resp. issue a prediction) if and only if σi=1\sigma_{i}=1 (resp. σi=0\sigma_{i}=0). In the case of linear classifiers, it is natural to base this choice on the margin (output) ⟨wi,xi⟩\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle of the model for the running sample xix_{i}. We thus model σi\sigma_{i} as a Bernoulli variable of law ℬ⁡(pi​(⟨wi,xi⟩))\mathcal{B}(p_{i}(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle)), where the sequence (pi)i∈[n](p_{i})_{i\in[n]} of functions pi:ℝ→[0,1]p_{i}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbb{R}\rightarrow[0,1] denotes the schedule of selection policies according to which the learner makes decisions. Note that we thus allow the policy to vary in time, and to be stochastic. Interestingly, the optimal policies derived below will correspond to deterministic selections, where pip_{i} takes values in {0,1}\{0,1\}. A particularly well-known instance of such deterministic rules are hard inner-margin rules pi(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤κ]p_{i}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\kappa] (Tong and Koller, 2001; Roth and Small, 2006), which prescribe to label samples whenever they fall within a certain distance κ\kappa of the decision boundary, with the intuition that the closest samples are the hardest to classify for the current model, hence the most informative. Many other margin-based policies tailored to online Adatron or perceptron learning were proposed in the literature, see for instance Dasgupta et al. (2005); Sculley (2007); Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2004), and Cacciarelli and Kulahci (2024) for a survey.

Cost metrics.

The present manuscript aims at ascertaining the optimal policy schedule pi​(⋅)p_{i}(\cdot). There exist two natural notions of cost with respect to which policies may be compared. The first is the final generalization error, defined as the misclassification error

εg,i=ℙ[⟨wi,x⟩y<0],\displaystyle\varepsilon_{g,i}=\mathbb{P}\left[\left\langle w_{i},x\right\rangle y<0\right], (2)

at the final round i=ni=n. In the above display, the probability bears over test samples x,yx,y from the same distribution as the stream of training samples. We investigate policies minimizing ϵg,n\epsilon_{g,n} with a constraint on the total number 𝒬n\mathcal{Q}_{n} of queried samples:

𝒬n≡∑i=1nσi=⌊γ​n⌋,\mathcal{Q}_{n}\equiv\sum\limits_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}=\lfloor\gamma\,n\rfloor, (3)

where γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] is the labeling budget. The final generalization error is the metric most often adopted in the active learning literature, and describes situations where the model is audited only post-training, when solely its final performance matters. To give an analogy in human learning, the same setup describes the situation of a student, whose performance at exercise sessions is inconsequential, provided they perform well at the final exam.

Selective sampling is, instead, concerned with controlling the cumulative number of errors and queries over training. If mistakes have unit cost while queries have relative cost Δ\Delta, the cumulative cost at round kk is

ℛk=1d​(ℳk+Δ​𝒬k).\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{k}=\frac{1}{d}\left(\mathcal{M}_{k}+\Delta~\mathcal{Q}_{k}\right)\,. (4)

The cumulative number of queries 𝒬k\mathcal{Q}_{k} is defined in (3) and the cumulative number of mistakes is given by

ℳk=∑i=1k(1−σi)𝟙[⟨wi,xi⟩yi<0].\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{k}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k}(1-\sigma_{i})\mathds{1}[\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle y_{i}<0]\,. (5)

For instance, in the case of medical diagnostics, a diagnosis needs to be presented to each patient, posing the challenge to properly balance the costs of a wrong diagnosis and that of asking for expensive human expertise.

Myopic and horizon-optimized rules.

Our analysis thus sets out to describe the horizon-optimized policies pϵ,i⋆p^{\star}_{\epsilon,i}, pℛ,i⋆p^{\star}_{\mathcal{R},i}, respectively minimizing the average error 𝔼⁡[ϵg,n]\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon_{g,n}\right] under a labeling budget γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] or the average total cumulative cost 𝔼⁡[ℛn]\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}_{n}\right]. From prior works in online learning in the high-dimensional regime n≍dn\asymp d (Saad and Solla, 1995a; Saad and Solla, 1995b; Goldt et al., 2019), one expects that for a given policy the random variables ϵg,n\epsilon_{g,n} and ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n} concentrate around their expectations as n,d→∞n,d\rightarrow\infty. Heuristically, policies resulting in small costs in expectation are thus also anticipated to display good performance on individual trials, as we illustrate in Figs. 1 (right) and 2 (right).

We also consider myopic policies, which at each round minimize the expected change of the objective, conditional on the model weights at the beginning of the round. Formally, the myopic policy pϵ,i∘p^{\circ}_{\epsilon,i} (resp. pℛ,i∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},i}) minimizes 𝔼⁡[ϵg,i+1−ϵg,i]\mathbb{E}\left[\epsilon_{g,i+1}-\epsilon_{g,i}\right] (resp. 𝔼⁡[ℛi+1−ℛi]\mathbb{E}\left[\mathcal{R}_{i+1}-\mathcal{R}_{i}\right]), where the expectation bears on the sample (xi,yi)(x_{i},y_{i}) and the query decision σi\sigma_{i}. Because they ignore the effect of the current choice on future rounds, myopic policies can prove suboptimal whenever queries that seem costly early in training pay off later on. For instance, for Δ>1/2\Delta>1/2 a myopic learner never queries, since random-chance error is 1/2<Δ1/2<\Delta. However, a strategy that minimizes the final cost ℛn\mathcal{R}_{n} could in principle query even at Δ>1/2\Delta>\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}. For simplicity, we focus on Δ<1/2\Delta<1/2 throughout.

2 Closed-form description of the training dynamics

In the high-dimensional regime d≫1d\gg 1, identifying optimal selection strategies is hampered by the curse of dimensionality. We circumvent this challenge by reducing the high-dimensional SGD dynamics in Eq. (1) to scalar ODEs bearing on a small set of summary statistics, also known as order parameters in statistical physics (Saad and Solla, 1995a). Following Mignacco and Mori (2026), we then apply standard control-theoretic methods to this low-dimensional description to find the optimal selection schedules.

Result 2.1 (Exact ODEs for the learning dynamics).

Let wiw_{i} denote the weights of the learner after ii steps of the online SGD dynamics in (1). In the limit d,i→∞d,i\rightarrow\infty with t=i/d=𝒪d​(1)t=\nicefrac{{i}}{{d}}=\mathcal{O}_{d}(1), the scalar summary statistics

mt=⟨wt​d,β⟩d,qt=⟨wt​d,wt​d⟩dm_{t}=\frac{\langle w_{td},\beta\rangle}{d}\,,\quad\quad q_{t}=\frac{\langle w_{td},w_{td}\rangle}{d} (6)

concentrate in probability to the solution at time tt of the following deterministic ODEs

dmtdt=fm​(mt,qt,pt),\displaystyle\frac{\differential m_{t}}{\differential t}=f_{m}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})\,, dqtdt=fq​(mt,qt,pt),\displaystyle\frac{\differential q_{t}}{\differential t}=f_{q}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})\,, (7)

where fmf_{m} and fqf_{q} are functions of mtm_{t} and qtq_{t} and functionals of the selection policy ptp_{t}. The expressions of fmf_{m} and fqf_{q} are given in App. A. We refer to tt as the training time and tF=n/dt_{F}=\nicefrac{{n}}{{d}} as the time horizon.

Fig. 5 in App. A shows that this theoretical prediction matches a single instance of numerical simulations already at d=1000d=1000. The ODEs capture the time evolution of the squared norm qtq_{t} of the weights and their overlap mtm_{t} with the ground truth vector β\beta. In the remainder of the paper, we work within this continuous-time description and, with a slight abuse of notation, index all quantities introduced in Sec. 1 by tt, e.g. ℛt=ℛt​d\mathcal{R}_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{td}.

Remark 2.2.

The cost metrics in Eq. (2) and (4) can be expressed as explicit functions of the summary statistics mtm_{t} and qtq_{t}. The generalization error is εg,t=1/π​arccos⁡(mt/qt).\varepsilon_{g,t}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{\pi}}\arccosop\!\left(\nicefrac{{m_{t}}}{{\sqrt{q}_{t}}}\right)\,. Similarly, the cumulative cost ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} (4) can be expressed as a function of the summary statistics mt′m_{t^{\prime}} and qt′q_{t^{\prime}} for t′∈[0,t]t^{\prime}\in[0,t], see App. A.

Since the cost metrics are determined by the summary statistics, which evolve according to the low-dimensional deterministic dynamics in Eq. (7), we can use control-theoretic methods to find optimal training strategies. When considering inner or intermediate-margin policies, we parametrize the selection thresholds as piecewise constant in time and optimize them by direct single shooting, using exact gradients obtained by automatic differentiation through the discretized ODEs in JAX (see App. B). The resulting problem is non-convex, so the schedules we obtain are not guaranteed to be global optima. Nevertheless, they consistently outperform all the benchmarks we consider.

3 Minimizing the final error

We first look for selection policies ptp_{t} that minimize the final generalization error εg,tF\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}} over a given time-horizon tFt_{F}, subject to the following continuous-time constraint on the total number of queries (cf. Eq. (3))

1tF​∫0tF𝔼⁡[pt​(ωt)]​dt=γ,\frac{1}{t_{F}}\int_{0}^{t_{F}}\!\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega_{t})]\,\differential t=\gamma\,, (8)

where 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] is the expected value w.r.t. ωt∼𝒩⁡(0,qt)\omega_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{t}).

3.1 Myopic policy pε,t∘p^{\circ}_{\varepsilon,t}

As a first step, we investigate the myopic policy that greedily maximizes at each step the decrease in generalization error −dεg,t/dt-\nicefrac{{\differential\varepsilon_{g,t}}}{{\differential t}}. This analysis will serve as a basis for designing the horizon-optimized policy that minimizes the terminal error εg,tF\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}}. Note however that such myopic policy would not satisfy the global constraint in Eq. (8). As a consequence, we introduce a modified myopic policy that depends on a single Lagrange multiplier ν\nu, enforcing (8) (see App. B).

Result 3.1 (Myopic policy under query budget).

The myopic policy is given by

pε,t∘(⋅)=𝟙[St(⋅)+ν<0],p^{\circ}_{\varepsilon,t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}\left[S_{t}(\cdot)+\nu<0\right]\,, (9)

where St​(⋅)S_{t}(\cdot) is given in Eq. (35) of App. B and ν>0\nu>0 is chosen to enforce Eq. (8). For a wide range of parameters this results in the intermediate-margin policy

pε,t∘(⋅)=𝟙[at≤|⋅|≤bt],p^{\circ}_{\varepsilon,t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[a_{t}\leq|\cdot|\leq b_{t}]\,, (10)

where the threshold values ata_{t} and btb_{t} are the positive roots of St​(ω)+ν=0S_{t}(\omega)+\nu=0 (see Fig. 6).

Interestingly, while inner-margin selection policies are most commonly studied in the literature, Res. 3.1 shows that selecting samples with intermediate margins can be more beneficial. We can interpret this policy by noting that the weight update (1) from the Adatron rule is proportional to the margin |ω||\omega| for misclassified samples. Samples with small margins therefore produce updates that are too small to justify spending the query budget on them. Conversely, at large |ω||\omega| samples are rarely misclassified, so a query there would also be uneconomical. Furthermore, although stochastic policies are allowed, the myopic policy is deterministic almost surely, because the instantaneous objective is linear in the selection probability (see App. B).

3.2 Horizon-optimized intermediate-margin policy pε,t⋆p^{\star}_{\varepsilon,t}

Motivated by the functional form of the myopic policy in Res. 3.1, we use control theory to identify the policy pε,t⋆p^{\star}_{\varepsilon,t} minimizing the final generalization error εg,tF\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}} within the class of intermediate-margin rules (for details, see App. B).

Result 3.2 (Horizon-optimized policy under query budget).

The horizon-optimized intermediate-margin policy is

pε,t⋆(⋅)=𝟙[at⋆≤|⋅|≤bt⋆],p^{\star}_{\varepsilon,t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[a^{\star}_{t}\leq|\cdot|\leq b^{\star}_{t}]\;, (11)

where the optimal thresholding schedule is given by

(at⋆,bt⋆)=argmin{at,bt}⁡εg,tF, subject to (8) .(a_{t}^{\star},b_{t}^{\star})=\operatorname{argmin}_{\{a_{t},b_{t}\}}\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}}\,,\text{ subject to \eqref{eq:budget}\,.} (12)

The minimization in Eq. (12) bears on 0≤at≤bt0\leq a_{t}\leq b_{t} for t∈[0,tF]t\in[0,t_{F}], resulting in the schedule in Fig. 1.

Fig. 1 (left) compares the myopic policy pε,t∘p^{\circ}_{\varepsilon,t} (10), in blue, with the horizon-optimized intermediate-margin policy pε,t⋆p^{\star}_{\varepsilon,t} (11), in yellow. Both schedules reduce the selection interval as training progresses and classification improves at smaller margins. However, the horizon-optimized schedule can exploit the full training horizon to restrict the selection interval from the beginning, whereas the myopic one starts by querying a much broader range of margins, that early in training yield substantial immediate improvements, but it exhausts the labeling budget before reaching tFt_{F}.

Fig. 1 (right) shows the final generalization error as a function of the query budget for pε,t∘p^{\circ}_{\varepsilon,t} and pε,t⋆p^{\star}_{\varepsilon,t}. As benchmarks, we include the (time and margin independent) random policy p=γp=\gamma, the constant intermediate-margin policy p(⋅)=𝟙[a⋆≤|⋅|≤b⋆]p(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[a^{\star}\leq|\cdot|\leq b^{\star}], and the inner-margin policy pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤κt⋆]p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\kappa_{t}^{\star}], with either a constant threshold κ⋆\kappa^{\star} or a schedule κt⋆\kappa^{\star}_{t}. All free parameters are optimized to minimize εg,tF\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}}. The optimal intermediate-margin schedule achieves the lowest final error, with the largest gains at small query budget γ\gamma. Even with constant thresholds, intermediate-margin selection outperforms constant and time-dependent inner-margin policies at small and moderate budgets γ\gamma. We note that this observed sub-optimality of inner-margin selections echoes the findings of Hacohen et al. (2022); Hacohen and Weinshall (2023); Kolossov et al. (2023); Cui and Lu (2026); Tifrea et al. (2023) in the pool-based setting.

4 Minimizing the cumulative cost

In this section, we now turn to studying policies minimizing the cumulative cost ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} (4). We show that both the myopic policy and the horizon-optimized intermediate-margin policy are inner-margin rules. Indeed, samples with small |ω||\omega| produce small weight updates and are thus discarded when the objective is the final error under a budget. However, these are also the samples the model is most likely to misclassify. If mistakes made during training are costly, querying them avoids a likely error, and this benefit outweighs the small size of the resulting update.

4.1 Myopic policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}

The following Result, derived in App. C, shows that the myopic policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} minimizing the instantaneous increase d/dt​ℛt\nicefrac{{\differential}}{{\differential t}}\mathcal{R}_{t} in cost (4) corresponds to a deterministic inner-margin policy (Tong and Koller, 2001; Roth and Small, 2006) with shrinking threshold.

Result 4.1 (Myopic policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} for the cumulative cost).

The myopic policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} is given by

pℛ,t∘(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤κt∘],\displaystyle p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\kappa^{\circ}_{t}], (13)

where the margin κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} reads

κt∘=qt∘​2​(qt∘/(mt∘)2−1)​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|,\displaystyle\kappa^{\circ}_{t}=\sqrt{q^{\circ}_{t}}\sqrt{2(\nicefrac{{q^{\circ}_{t}}}{{(m^{\circ}_{t})^{2}}}-1)}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|, (14)

with qt∘,mt∘q^{\circ}_{t},m^{\circ}_{t} satisfying self-consistently the equations (7) with policy pt=pℛ,t∘p_{t}=p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}. As t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, for η=2\eta=2, the threshold κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} shrinks asymptotically as

κt∘=q0​c​(Δ)t+o⁡(1t),\displaystyle\kappa^{\circ}_{t}=\frac{\sqrt{q_{0}}\,c(\Delta)}{t}+o\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\,, (15)

where c⁡(Δ)>0c(\Delta)>0 is given in Eq. (63) in App. C.

As in Sec. 3, we find a deterministic policy because the instantaneous objective is linear in ptp_{t}. This simple policy notably induces a sub-linear growth for cost metrics, and logarithmic label complexity, as formalized in the following remark.

Remark 4.2.

Under the myopic policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} characterized in Result 4.1, for η=2\eta=2, the cumulative cost ℛt∘\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}, number of mistakes ℳt∘\mathcal{M}^{\circ}_{t} and number of queries 𝒬t∘\mathcal{Q}^{\circ}_{t} scale logarithmically with training time:

ℛt∘,ℳt∘,𝒬t∘≍ln⁡t.\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{t}^{\circ},\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\circ},\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\circ}\asymp\ln t\,. (16)

The error scales as εg,t∘≍1/t\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\circ}\asymp\nicefrac{{1}}{{t}}, and thus decays exponentially with the number of queries 𝒬t∘\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\circ}. These scalings match for example those reported in Yan and Zhang (2017); Huang et al. (2022); Cavallanti et al. (2008).

4.2 Horizon-optimized intermediate-margin policy pℛ,t⋆p^{\star}_{\mathcal{R},t}

We now turn to the horizon-optimized policy pℛ,t⋆p^{\star}_{\mathcal{R},t} for the cumulative cost, again focusing on the class of intermediate-margin strategies, as for Res. 3.2.

Result 4.3 (Horizon-optimized policy for the cumulative cost).

We again optimize an intermediate-margin policy

pℛ,t⋆(⋅)=𝟙[at⋆≤|⋅|≤bt⋆],p^{\star}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[a^{\star}_{t}\leq|\cdot|\leq b^{\star}_{t}]\;, (17)

where the optimal thresholding schedule is given by

(at⋆,bt⋆)=argmin{at,bt}⁡ℛtF.(a_{t}^{\star},b_{t}^{\star})=\operatorname{argmin}_{\{a_{t},b_{t}\}}\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}}\,. (18)

For all parameter values considered, we obtain at⋆=0a^{\star}_{t}=0, so that the horizon-optimized strategy collapses onto an inner-margin policy. This collapse is shown in Fig. 2 (right) and largely extends to time independent policies.

Fig. 2 (right) shows that time-dependent schedules achieve lower cost than the best random policy pt​(⋅)=pp_{t}(\cdot)=p and all constant strategies. All free parameters, including pp, are chosen to minimize ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}}. The horizon-optimized schedule outperforms the myopic one, with a gap growing with Δ\Delta. The myopic rule queries only when it lowers the cost immediately, ignoring that each query also reduces future mistakes. At large Δ\Delta it therefore queries too little, whereas the horizon-optimized schedule invests in queries early in training that pay off later on.

4.3 Experiments

The particularly compact asymptotic form (15) for the myopic threshold (13) naturally inspires the simple heuristic policy schedule pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤K/t],p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\nicefrac{{K}}{{t}}], with a threshold shrinking at a 1/t\nicefrac{{1}}{{t}} rate. We compare the performance of this policy against other margin-based rules for online Adatron/Perceptron learning proposed in the literature. Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2004) –blue lines in Fig. 3– (resp. Sculley (2007) –green lines in Fig. 3–) propose a sigmoid (resp. exponential) functional ansatz for the selection probability pt​(⋅)p_{t}(\cdot). Orange lines represent a variant of the former rule, with adaptive bandwidth (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004). Dasgupta et al. (2005) –red lines in Fig. 3– on the other hand rely on a hard inner-margin selection rule pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤κt]p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\kappa_{t}] with an adaptive threshold that halves after every streak of consecutive correct predictions. Details on these algorithms and their implementation are collected within App. D. Fig. 3 (left) illustrates the time evolution of the cumulative cost ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} for these different policies, presenting only the choice of hyperparameter that minimizes in hindsight the terminal cost ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}}. The heuristic pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤K/t]p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\nicefrac{{K}}{{t}}] inspired from the t→∞t\rightarrow\infty asymptotics of Result 4.1 –brown lines in Fig. 3– compares favorably against the aforementioned baselines, and results in overall small cumulative cost ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t}. The performance for the particular prescription K∘=q0​c​(Δ)K^{\circ}=\sqrt{q_{0}}\,c(\Delta) for the hyperparameter KK, which can be read from the theoretical expression (15), is on the other hand found to deteriorate at larger costs Δ\Delta, as illustrated in Figs. 7 and 9 in App. D.

This observation stands in coherence with the discussion of the previous subsection that the performance of the myopic policy comparatively degrades at larger Δ\Delta, see Fig. 2 (right). A finer examination of the joint evolution of ℳt,𝒬t\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{Q}_{t} (Fig. 3, inset) reveals that the shrinking threshold K/t\nicefrac{{K}}{{t}} incentivizes a first phase of exploration, with a sharp increase of the number of queries 𝒬t\mathcal{Q}_{t}, followed by a phase of exploitation where the model attempts more predictions, as signaled by a sharp increase in mistakes ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t}. This qualitative behavior can still be observed for real data that does not satisfy the Gaussian assumption, as shown in Fig. 3 (right) for the task of pneumonia diagnosis from chest X-ray images (Kermany et al., 2018), and in Fig. 8 in App. D for Covid-19 diagnosis (Chowdhury et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2021).

4.4 Comments for two-layer neural networks

The findings of Sec. 4 make it tempting to wonder whether output-thresholding strategies are generically well-adapted to control the cumulative cost ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} (4). This final section nuances this picture, and shows that this intuition ceases to hold for more complex learning models. Consider for instance the width-rr two-layer neural network f(⋅)=v⊤g(W⋅)f(\cdot)=v^{\top}g\left(W\cdot\right) with weights v∈ℝr,W∈ℝr×dv\in\mathbb{R}^{r},W\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d}, and activation function gg acting entry-wise. We again consider training this model on the classification task described in Sec. 1, using online SGD (1). Note that when r=Θd​(1)r=\Theta_{d}(1) as n≍dn\asymp d diverge, the resulting training dynamics are again captured by a limiting set of low-dimensional ODEs (Saad and Solla, 1995a; Goldt et al., 2019). For such models, it is natural to consider the larger class of selection policies pt:ℝr→[0,1]p_{t}\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbb{R}^{r}\rightarrow[0,1] that take as argument for a given input xx the whole array of pre-activations W​xWx, rather than the sole output f⁡(x)f(x). We note that policies bearing exclusively over the output in fact correspond to special instances of the former class. Is the myopic policy for the cumulative cost still of the form of a hard-thresholding (13) on the output f⁡(x)f(x)? The next Result, derived in App. C, answers this question negatively.

Result 4.4 (Myopic policy for two-layer networks).

Conditional on the weights v,Wv,W at time tt, supposing WW is full rank and β∉rowsp⁡(W)\beta\notin{\rm rowsp}(W), the myopic policy for the cumulative cost at time tt is given by

pℛ,t∘(⋅)=𝟙[Φ(−sign(v⊤g(⋅))M⊤Q−1⋅1−M⊤​Q−1​M)≥Δ],\displaystyle\hskip-8.99994ptp^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}\left[\Phi\left(\frac{-\mathrm{sign}(v^{\top}g(\cdot))M^{\top}Q^{-1}\cdot}{\sqrt{1-M^{\top}Q^{-1}M}}\right)\geq\Delta\right], (19)

where M≔W​β/d∈ℝrM\coloneqq\nicefrac{{W\beta}}{{d}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} and Q≔W​W⊤/d∈ℝr×rQ\coloneqq\nicefrac{{WW^{\top}}}{{d}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}. Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) is the normal cumulative distribution function.

While the optimal policy is still found to be deterministic, it no longer depends on the pre-activation W​xWx through the sole output v⊤​g​(W​x)v^{\top}g(Wx). In fact, the regions in pre-activation space that the (oracle) policy (19) prescribes to select can significantly differ from those selected by a naive output-thresholding strategy of the form 𝟙[|v⊤g(⋅)|≤κ]\mathds{1}[|v^{\top}g(\cdot)|\leq\kappa]. Fig. 4 shows, for a g=GeLUg=\mathrm{GeLU} network with r=2r=2 hidden neurons trained without data selection on the logistic loss for 10001000 steps, that the two regions (respectively in blue and yellow) might in fact barely overlap.

Conclusions

We investigate data selection schedules for online active learning with linear classifiers. In the high- dimensional realizable Gaussian setup, we precisely characterize the margin-based selection policy schedules that minimize at each round the increment in error or cost of mistakes and queries, down to the constant. In many instances, we find that optimal strategies coincide with deterministic inner- or intermediate-margin selection rules with shrinking thresholds. Within these classes of policies, we further numerically determine the optimal threshold schedules that minimize the final error under a labeling budget or the cumulative cost. Finally, we exemplify how optimal selection policies for two-layer neural networks can take a more complex form. We believe that a precise investigation of the latter constitutes an interesting avenue for future research.

Limitations and perspectives

The theoretical contributions of the present work primarily describe linear classifiers, and moreover rest on strong assumptions, notably that of an isotropic Gaussian data distribution. It would be interesting to extend our analysis to models in which the input distribution itself encodes task-relevant structure, such as the hidden manifold model (Goldt et al., 2020) or class-dependent Gaussian mixtures (Refinetti et al., 2021), in order to investigate how this additional information affects query selection. Furthermore, we restricted ourselves to query policies that are functions of the sample margin (equivalently, model output) ⟨wi,xi⟩\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle. While this class encompasses many heuristics in the literature (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004; Sculley, 2007), there exist functionally more intricate policies that do not fall therein, such as the second-order rule of Cesa-Bianchi et al. (2004) (Fig. 3). Finally, while we focused on a single stationary task, a promising direction would be to investigate how to allocate a limited labeling budget across tasks in multi-task settings. Building on Mori et al. (2025), this could clarify how task similarity and interference affect optimal labeling strategies at different stages of learning.

Appendix A Derivation of the ODEs

In this appendix, we derive the ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the order parameters mm and qq given in Eq. (7) of the main text, tracking the learning dynamics of online SGD:

wi+1=wi−η​σi​ℓ′​(⟨wi,xi⟩​yi)​yi​xi,\displaystyle w_{i+1}=w_{i}-\eta\sigma_{i}\ell^{\prime}(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle y_{i})y_{i}x_{i}, (20)

with learning rate η>0\eta>0. The teacher β∈ℝd\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is fixed throughout the training, with ‖β‖22=d\|\beta\|^{2}_{2}=d, and the labels are yi=sign(⟨β,xi⟩)y_{i}=\sgn(\left\langle\beta,x_{i}\right\rangle). At each step ii, the selection process is encoded by the Bernoulli variable σi∼ℬ⁡(pi​(⟨wi,xi⟩))\sigma_{i}\sim\mathcal{B}(p_{i}(\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle)). In the following, we will consider differentiable losses ℓ:ℝ→ℝ+\ell\mathrel{\mathop{\mathchar 58\relax}}\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{+} of the signed margin, highlighting the Adatron rule with ℓ⁡(z)=1/2​min⁡(z,0)2\ell(z)=\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}\min(z,0)^{2} as a special case.

In the online setup, at each step ii a fresh sample xi∼𝒩⁡(0d,Id/d)x_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0_{d},I_{d}/d) is considered, independent of the weights wiw_{i}. Therefore, conditional on wiw_{i}, the margins (ωi∗,ωi)=(⟨β,xi⟩,⟨wi,xi⟩)(\omega^{*}_{i},\omega_{i})=(\left\langle\beta,x_{i}\right\rangle,\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle) are also jointly Gaussian with zero mean and second moments given by:

𝔼⁡[(ωi∗)2]=⟨β,β⟩d=1,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[(\omega_{i}^{*})^{2}\right]=\frac{\left\langle\beta,\beta\right\rangle}{d}=1\;, 𝔼⁡[ωi2]=⟨wi,wi⟩d≔qi,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\omega_{i}^{2}\right]=\frac{\left\langle w_{i},w_{i}\right\rangle}{d}\coloneqq q_{i}\;, 𝔼⁡[ωi∗​ωi]=⟨β,wi⟩d≔mi,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\omega_{i}^{*}\,\omega_{i}\right]=\frac{\left\langle\beta,w_{i}\right\rangle}{d}\coloneqq m_{i}\,, (21)

where the expectations are over xix_{i}, conditional on wiw_{i}. We have defined the order parameters mim_{i} (alignment with the teacher) and qiq_{i} (squared norm of the weights), which fully determine the joint conditional margin distribution

(ω∗,ω)∼𝒩⁡([00],[1mmq]).(\omega^{*},\omega)\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1&m\\ m&q\end{bmatrix}\right)\,. (22)

The generalization error depends on the weights only through the margins (ω∗,ω)(\omega^{*},\omega) and can thus be expressed solely in terms of the correlation coefficient m/q\nicefrac{{m}}{{\sqrt{q}}}

εg=ℙ[ωω∗<0]=1πarccos(mq).\varepsilon_{g}=\mathbb{P}\left[\omega\,\omega^{*}<0\right]=\frac{1}{\pi}\arccos\left(\frac{m}{\sqrt{q}}\right)\,. (23)

Therefore, in order to track the generalization error over training, it is sufficient to track the dynamics of the order parameters. Substituting the update rules (20) into the definitions (21) gives the exact increments

mi+1−mi=−ηd​σi​ℓ′​(ωi​yi)​yi​ωi∗,qi+1−qi=−2​ηd​σi​ℓ′​(ωi​yi)​yi​ωi+η2d​σi​(ℓ′​(ωi​yi))2​⟨xi,xi⟩,m_{i+1}-m_{i}=-\frac{\eta}{d}\sigma_{i}\ell^{\prime}(\omega_{i}y_{i})y_{i}\omega^{*}_{i}\;,\qquad q_{i+1}-q_{i}=-2\frac{\eta}{d}\sigma_{i}\ell^{\prime}(\omega_{i}y_{i})y_{i}\omega_{i}+\frac{\eta^{2}}{d}\sigma_{i}(\ell^{\prime}(\omega_{i}y_{i}))^{2}\left\langle x_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle\;, (24)

where we have used that σi∈{0,1}\sigma_{i}\in\{0,1\}, hence σi2=σi\sigma_{i}^{2}=\sigma_{i}. The quadratic term in the increment of qq must be retained, since it contributes at the same order in 1/d\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}} as the linear term.

We take the proportional infinite-dimensional limit d,n→∞d,n\rightarrow\infty with tF=n/dt_{F}=\nicefrac{{n}}{{d}} fixed and consider the macroscopic time t=i/d∈[0,tF]t=\nicefrac{{i}}{{d}}\in[0,t_{F}], where each increment is of order d​t=1/d{\rm d}t=\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}. The learning rate η\eta is also held fixed. The input norm satisfies 𝔼⁡[⟨xi,xi⟩]=1\mathbb{E}[\left\langle x_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle]=1 and Var⁡(⟨xi,xi⟩)=2/d\operatorname{Var}(\left\langle x_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle)=\nicefrac{{2}}{{d}}, and hence it converges in probability: ⟨xi,xi⟩→d→∞ℙ1\left\langle x_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle\xrightarrow[d\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}1. For an isotropic Gaussian initialization w0∼𝒩⁡(0,qinit​Id)w_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q_{\mathrm{init}}I_{d}) independent of the teacher, the initial order parameters also concentrate as d→∞d\rightarrow\infty. Indeed, averaging over the initialization and using ‖β‖2=d\|\beta\|^{2}=d,

𝔼⁡[m0]=0,Var⁡(m0)=qinitd,𝔼⁡[q0]=qinit,Var⁡(q0)=2​qinit2d.\mathbb{E}[m_{0}]=0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(m_{0})=\frac{q_{\mathrm{init}}}{d},\qquad\mathbb{E}[q_{0}]=q_{\mathrm{init}},\qquad\operatorname{Var}(q_{0})=\frac{2q_{\mathrm{init}}^{2}}{d}. (25)

Consequently, (m0,q0)→d→∞ℙ(0,qinit)(m_{0},q_{0})\xrightarrow[d\rightarrow\infty]{\mathbb{P}}(0,q_{\mathrm{init}}), providing deterministic initial conditions for the limiting dynamics.

To control the increments during training, we consider losses that satisfy |ℓ′​(z)|≤C⁡(1+|z|)|\ell^{\prime}(z)|\leq C(1+|z|) for all z∈ℝz\in\mathbb{R}, with a finite constant C>0C>0 independent of zz and dd. This encompasses squared hinge, square, and logistic losses. The increments in Eq. (24) scale as d−1d^{-1}. Over i=d​ti=d\,t steps at fixed tt, their conditional means generate a finite drift, while the centered fluctuations are uncorrelated across steps and have cumulative standard deviation of order d−1/2d^{-1/2}, vanishing as d→∞d\rightarrow\infty. Here, conditioning is on the training history before step ii, and the averages are over the fresh input xix_{i} and query decision σi\sigma_{i}.

The limiting dynamics are therefore determined by the conditional mean increments, following the standard ODE approach to online learning Saad and Solla (1995a); Biehl and Schwarze (1995); Engel and van den Broeck (2001) (see, e.g., (Goldt et al., 2019; Arous et al., 2021) for a more rigorous treatment). Averaging over σi\sigma_{i} replaces it by pi​(ωi)p_{i}(\omega_{i}), while input-norm concentration allows to replace ⟨xi,xi⟩\left\langle x_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle by one. Dividing the resulting mean increments by dt=1/d\differential t=\nicefrac{{1}}{{d}}, the order parameters dynamics (24) concentrate in probability to their deterministic limit

dmdt=fm​(mt,qt,pt)=−η​𝔼​[pt​(ω)​ℓ′​(ω​y)​y​ω∗],dqdt=fq​(mt,qt,pt)=−2​η​𝔼​[pt​(ω)​ℓ′​(ω​y)​y​ω]+η2​𝔼​[pt​(ω)​(ℓ′​(ω​y))2].\begin{split}\frac{\differential m}{\differential t}&=f_{m}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})=-\eta\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)\ell^{\prime}(\omega y)y\omega^{*}]\;,\\ \frac{\differential q}{\differential t}&=f_{q}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})=-2\eta\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)\ell^{\prime}(\omega y)y\omega]+\eta^{2}\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)(\ell^{\prime}(\omega y))^{2}].\end{split} (26)

At a fixed training time tt, we write m=mtm=m_{t} and q=qtq=q_{t}. Since the policy depends only on the margin ω\omega, it is convenient to first average over the conditional teacher margin ω∗|ω∼𝒩⁡(μ,s2)\omega^{*}\mid\omega\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,s^{2}), where μ=(m/q)​ω\mu=(\nicefrac{{m}}{{q}})\omega and s=1−m2/qs=\sqrt{1-m^{2}/q}. Denoting the standard normal density (resp. cumulative distribution function) as GG (resp. Φ\Phi), the marginal density of ω\omega as PqP_{q}, and its standardized conditional mean as ζ\zeta,

G⁡(x)=e−x2/22​π,Φ⁡(x)=∫−∞xG⁡(u)​du,Pq​(ω)=e−ω2/(2q)2​π​q,ζ=μs=m​ωq⁡(q−m2),\displaystyle G(x)=\frac{e^{-x^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},\quad\Phi(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}\!G(u)\,\differential u,\quad P_{q}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\omega^{2}/(2q)}}{\sqrt{2\pi q}},\quad\zeta=\frac{\mu}{s}=\frac{m\,\omega}{\sqrt{q(q-m^{2})}}\,, (27)

the three moments appearing in Eq. (26) are given by

𝔼⁡[(ℓ′​(ω​y))2∣ω]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[(\ell^{\prime}(\omega y))^{2}\mid\omega] =Φ⁡(ζ)​ℓ′​(ω)2+Φ⁡(−ζ)​ℓ′​(−ω)2,\displaystyle=\Phi(\zeta)\,\ell^{\prime}(\omega)^{2}+\Phi(-\zeta)\,\ell^{\prime}(-\omega)^{2}, (28)
𝔼⁡[ℓ′​(ω​y)​y​ω∣ω]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\ell^{\prime}(\omega y)y\,\omega\mid\omega] =ω⁡[Φ⁡(ζ)​ℓ′​(ω)−Φ⁡(−ζ)​ℓ′​(−ω)],\displaystyle=\omega\big[\Phi(\zeta)\,\ell^{\prime}(\omega)-\Phi(-\zeta)\,\ell^{\prime}(-\omega)\big], (29)
𝔼⁡[ℓ′​(ω​y)​y​ω∗∣ω]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\ell^{\prime}(\omega y)y\,\omega^{\ast}\mid\omega] =ℓ′​(ω)​(μ​Φ​(ζ)+s​G​(ζ))−ℓ′​(−ω)​(μ​Φ​(−ζ)−s​G​(ζ)).\displaystyle=\ell^{\prime}(\omega)\big(\mu\Phi(\zeta)+sG(\zeta)\big)-\ell^{\prime}(-\omega)\big(\mu\Phi(-\zeta)-sG(\zeta)\big). (30)

For any function h⁡(ω,ω∗)h(\omega,\omega^{*}), the corresponding term in (26) factorizes as

𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)​h​(ω,ω∗)]=∫−∞∞dω​Pq​(ω)​pt​(ω)​𝔼​[h⁡(ω,ω∗)|ω].\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)h(\omega,\omega^{*})]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q}(\omega)\,p_{t}(\omega)\,\mathbb{E}[h(\omega,\omega^{*})|\omega]\;. (31)

All three moments in (30) are even in ω\omega, so every policy that we derive in the following can be written as a condition on |ω||\omega| alone.

For the Adatron rule, ℓ′​(z)=min⁡(z,0)\ell^{\prime}(z)=\min(z,0), so yℓ′(ωy)=ω𝟏{ωω∗<0}y\ell^{\prime}(\omega y)=\omega\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega\omega^{*}<0\}} and (ℓ′(ωy))2=ω2𝟏{ωω∗<0}(\ell^{\prime}(\omega y))^{2}=\omega^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\{\omega\omega^{*}<0\}}. Each nonzero update increases the overlap mm, therefore, starting from m0=0m_{0}=0, we have m≥0m\geq 0 nondecreasing throughout training. Using the conditional misclassification probability ℙ⁡[ω​ω∗<0∣ω]=Φ⁡(−|ζ|)\mathbb{P}[\omega\omega^{*}<0\mid\omega]=\Phi(-|\zeta|) for ω≠0\omega\neq 0, Eq. (26) becomes

fm​(mt,qt,pt)=η​∫−∞∞dω​Pqt​(ω)​pt​(ω)​[st​|ω|​G​(ζt)−mtqt​ω2​Φ​(−|ζt|)],fq​(mt,qt,pt)=η⁡(η−2)​∫−∞∞dω​Pqt​(ω)​pt​(ω)​ω2​Φ​(−|ζt|).\displaystyle\begin{split}f_{m}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})&=\eta\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q_{t}}(\omega)p_{t}(\omega)\left[s_{t}|\omega|G(\zeta_{t})-\frac{m_{t}}{q_{t}}\omega^{2}\Phi(-|\zeta_{t}|)\right]\,,\\ f_{q}(m_{t},q_{t};p_{t})&=\eta(\eta-2)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q_{t}}(\omega)p_{t}(\omega)\omega^{2}\Phi(-|\zeta_{t}|)\,.\end{split} (32)

The self-overlap qtq_{t} is nonincreasing for 0<η<20<\eta<2 and remains constant for η=2\eta=2 in the limiting dynamics.

Figure 5 compares the ODE predictions (32) with numerical simulations of a single SGD trajectory at d=1000d=1000 under the fixed policy pt(ω)=𝟏{|ω|<1}p_{t}(\omega)=\mathbf{1}_{\{|\omega|<1\}}. During training, the overlap mtm_{t} increases while the normalized squared weight norm qtq_{t} decreases, increasing their correlation mt/qtm_{t}/\sqrt{q_{t}} and thereby reducing the generalization error. The close agreement between the theoretical curves and simulation points shows that the ODEs accurately capture this evolution already at finite dimension.

Similarly, we derive the dynamics of the (rescaled) cumulative cost ℛk=(ℳk+Δ​𝒬k)/d{\cal R}_{k}={(\mathcal{M}_{k}+\Delta\,{\cal Q}_{k})}/d (see Eq. (4) of the main text) by averaging its one-step increments over the fresh input xix_{i} and query decision σi\sigma_{i}, conditional on the training history before step ii. We recall that 𝒬k=∑i=1kσi{\cal Q}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i} denotes the cumulative number of queries, and ℳk=∑i=1k(1−σi)𝟙[ωiyi<0]{\cal M}_{k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(1-\sigma_{i})\mathds{1}[\omega_{i}y_{i}<0] the cumulative number of mistakes. Since dd samples arrive per unit of macroscopic time, with a slight abuse of notation here we denote by 𝒬t{\cal Q}_{t} and ℳt{\cal M}_{t} the deterministic limits of 𝒬k/d\mathcal{Q}_{k}/d, ℳk/d\mathcal{M}_{k}/d at k=⌊d​t⌋k=\lfloor d\,t\rfloor, while ℛt=ℛ⌊d​t⌋\mathcal{R}_{t}=\mathcal{R}_{\lfloor d\,t\rfloor} as in the main text. Their time evolution is given by

𝒬t=∫0tdt′​∫−∞∞dω​Pqt′​(ω)​pt′​(ω),ℳt=∫0tdt′​∫−∞∞dω​Pqt′​(ω)​[1−pt′​(ω)]​Φ​(−|ζt′|),ℛt=ℳt+Δ​𝒬t,\begin{split}{\cal Q}_{t}&=\int_{0}^{t}\differential t^{\prime}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q_{t^{\prime}}}(\omega)p_{t^{\prime}}(\omega)\,,\\ {\cal M}_{t}&=\int_{0}^{t}\differential t^{\prime}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q_{t^{\prime}}}(\omega)[1-p_{t^{\prime}}(\omega)]\Phi(-|\zeta_{t^{\prime}}|),\\ {\cal R}_{t}&={\cal M}_{t}+\Delta\,{\cal Q}_{t}\,,\end{split} (33)

The constraint that a fraction γ\gamma of the samples is queried becomes

𝒬tFtF=1tF​∫0tFdt​∫−∞∞dω​Pqt​(ω)​pt​(ω)=γ.\frac{{\cal Q}_{t_{F}}}{t_{F}}=\frac{1}{t_{F}}\int_{0}^{t_{F}}\differential t\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\differential\omega\,P_{q_{t}}(\omega)p_{t}(\omega)=\gamma\,. (34)

Appendix B Control methods

The ODEs of Result 2.1 reduce the search for a selection policy to a low-dimensional optimal control problem. The state is (mt,qt)(m_{t},q_{t}), the control is the policy ptp_{t}, and the objective is either the final error εg,tF\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}} under the budget (8), or the cumulative cost ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}}. This appendix describes how we solve this problem. We first derive the myopic policy, then explain how we discretize and optimize time-dependent schedules.

B.1 Myopic policies

Both fmf_{m} and fqf_{q} are linear in ptp_{t}, so the rate of change of the error is linear in ptp_{t} as well. We can write it as

dεgdt=𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)​St​(ω)],St​(ω)=∂εg∂m​δ​fmδ​pt​(ω)+∂εg∂q​δ​fqδ​pt​(ω),\frac{\differential\varepsilon_{g}}{\differential t}=\mathbb{E}\big[p_{t}(\omega)\,S_{t}(\omega)\big],\qquad S_{t}(\omega)=\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{g}}{\partial m}\,\frac{\delta f_{m}}{\delta p_{t}(\omega)}+\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{g}}{\partial q}\,\frac{\delta f_{q}}{\delta p_{t}(\omega)}, (35)

where ∂εg/∂m=−1/(πq−m2)\partial\varepsilon_{g}/\partial m=-1/(\pi\sqrt{q-m^{2}}) and ∂εg/∂q=m/(2​π​q​q−m2)\partial\varepsilon_{g}/\partial q=m/(2\pi q\sqrt{q-m^{2}}) follow from (23). We recall that 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes the expected value with respect to ω∼𝒩⁡(0,q)\omega\sim\mathcal{N}(0,q). The function St​(ω)S_{t}(\omega) measures how much querying a sample at margin ω\omega changes dεg/dt\differential\varepsilon_{g}/\differential t. Samples with St​(ω)<0S_{t}(\omega)<0 reduce the error, and the others do not. A greedy policy that minimizes (35) at each time would therefore query every ω\omega with St​(ω)<0S_{t}(\omega)<0. For the Adatron rule, however, StS_{t} is negative for all ω>0\omega>0. The greedy policy then queries every sample and violates the budget (8).

To enforce the budget, we introduce a Lagrange multiplier ν≥0\nu\geq 0. This is a single scalar for the whole trajectory, and it acts as a fixed price per query. The instantaneous objective 𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)​(St​(ω)+ν)]\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)(S_{t}(\omega)+\nu)] is linear in ptp_{t}. Therefore, optimizing over arbitrary selection probabilities yields a deterministic myopic schedule almost surely: a sample at margin ω\omega is queried only if St​(ω)+ν<0S_{t}(\omega)+\nu<0, that is, only if the error reduction it brings outweighs the price of the query, giving the policy of Result 3.1. We tune ν\nu by bisection so that the realized query rate equals γ\gamma.

B.2 Quadrature on the selected intervals

All the policies we consider select a union of intervals in |ω||\omega|, and the integrands in fmf_{m} and fqf_{q} are even in ω\omega. For an intermediate-margin policy pt(ω)=𝟙[at≤|ω|≤bt]p_{t}(\omega)=\mathds{1}[a_{t}\leq|\omega|\leq b_{t}], every expectation is therefore an ordinary integral over the selected interval:

𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)​X​(ω)]=2​∫atbtdω​Pqt​(ω)​X​(ω),Pq​(ω)=e−ω2/2q2​π​q,\mathbb{E}\big[p_{t}(\omega)\,X(\omega)\big]=2\int_{a_{t}}^{b_{t}}\!\differential\omega\;P_{q_{t}}(\omega)\,X(\omega),\qquad P_{q}(\omega)=\frac{e^{-\omega^{2}/2q}}{\sqrt{2\pi q}}\,, (36)

where XX stands for any of the conditional moments of App. A. We compute these integrals with an nn-point Gauss–Legendre rule, rescaled from [−1,1][-1,1] to [at,bt][a_{t},b_{t}]:

ωj=at+bt2+bt−at2​ξj,𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)​X​(ω)]≃(bt−at)​∑j=1nWj​Pqt​(ωj)​X​(ωj),\omega_{j}=\frac{a_{t}+b_{t}}{2}+\frac{b_{t}-a_{t}}{2}\,\xi_{j},\qquad\mathbb{E}\big[p_{t}(\omega)\,X(\omega)\big]\simeq(b_{t}-a_{t})\sum_{j=1}^{n}W_{j}\,P_{q_{t}}(\omega_{j})\,X(\omega_{j}), (37)

where {ξj}\{\xi_{j}\} and {Wj}\{W_{j}\} are the standard Gauss–Legendre nodes and weights on [−1,1][-1,1]. This choice has two advantages. First, it is very accurate. The integrand Pqt​XP_{q_{t}}X is analytic on [at,bt][a_{t},b_{t}], so the quadrature error decreases geometrically with nn and we use n=48n=48. Second, and more importantly, it makes the discretized ODE in Eq. (37) differentiable with respect to the policy parameter ata_{t} and btb_{t}.

B.3 Piecewise-constant schedules

For simplicity, we approximate the schedules to be piecewise constant in time. We split the horizon into NcN_{c} equal blocks and keep the radii fixed within each block:

at=ak,bt=bkfort∈[(k−1)​tFNc,k​tFNc),k=1,…,Nc.a_{t}=a_{k},\quad b_{t}=b_{k}\qquad\text{for}\quad t\in\Big[\tfrac{(k-1)t_{F}}{N_{c}},\,\tfrac{k\,t_{F}}{N_{c}}\Big),\qquad k=1,\dots,N_{c}. (38)

The control is then a vector of 2​Nc2N_{c} numbers, or NcN_{c} numbers for inner-margin policies, where ak≡0a_{k}\equiv 0. We integrate the ODEs (7) with forward Euler on NsN_{s} time steps, with NsN_{s} a multiple of NcN_{c}. The time integrals in (8) and in ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} are computed with the trapezoidal rule on the same grid. During optimization we use Nc=50N_{c}=50 and Ns=500N_{s}=500. All reported quantities are then recomputed with Ns=2000N_{s}=2000.

B.4 Enforcing the query budget

During optimization, we impose the budget (8) through a quadratic penalty:

ℒ=εg,tF+ρ​(1tF​∫0tF𝔼⁡[pt​(ω)]​dt−γ)2,ρ=300.\mathcal{L}=\varepsilon_{g,t_{F}}+\rho\left(\frac{1}{t_{F}}\int_{0}^{t_{F}}\!\mathbb{E}[p_{t}(\omega)]\,\differential t-\gamma\right)^{2},\qquad\rho=300. (39)

A penalty does not enforce the constraint exactly, so the optimized schedule can slightly overspend or underspend the budget. We correct this afterwards by rescaling all interval widths by a common factor ss, bk↦→ak+s⁡(bk−ak)b_{k}\mapstochar\rightarrow a_{k}+s\,(b_{k}-a_{k}), with ss chosen by bisection so that the query rate equals γ\gamma. We then recompute the error for the corrected schedule.

B.5 Optimization

We solve the resulting finite-dimensional problem by direct single shooting: for a given control vector, we simulate the whole trajectory, evaluate the objective, and update the controls. The forward simulation is implemented in JAX, which provides exact gradients with respect to the control vector by reverse-mode automatic differentiation through the discretized trajectory. We minimize with L-BFGS-B, using box constraints on the controls. The objective has several local minima, so we run each optimization from a few initializations, and we warm-start from the previous solution when sweeping γ\gamma or Δ\Delta. We report the best local optimum found.

Appendix C Myopic schedules for the cumulative cost

We detail in this Appendix the derivations of the myopic policy for the cumulative cost objective ℛt\mathcal{R}_{t} (4), for a linear classifier (Res. 4.1) and a two-layer neural network (Res.  4.4).

C.1 Linear classifier

We first ascertain the policy schedule pℛ,t∘​(⋅)p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\cdot) that greedily minimizes the local increment in cost d/dt​ℛt\nicefrac{{\differential}}{{\differential t}}\mathcal{R}_{t}. At a given step tt, the latter reads

dℛtdt=Δ𝔼[pt(ω)]+𝔼[(1−pt(ω))𝟙[ωω∗<0]],\displaystyle\frac{\differential\mathcal{R}_{t}}{\differential t}=\Delta\mathbb{E}\left[p_{t}(\omega)\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[(1-p_{t}(\omega))\mathds{1}[\omega\omega^{\ast}<0\right]], (40)

where the expectation bears over

ω,ω∗∼𝒩⁡(02,[qtmtmt1]).\displaystyle\omega,\omega^{\ast}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0_{2},\begin{bmatrix}q_{t}&m_{t}\\ m_{t}&1\end{bmatrix}\right). (41)

For a given ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}, taking a functional derivative with respect to pt​(ω)p_{t}(\omega),

δδ​pt​(ω)​dℛtdt\displaystyle\frac{\delta}{\delta p_{t}(\omega)}\frac{\differential\mathcal{R}_{t}}{\differential t} =e−ω22​qt∘2​π​qt[Δ−𝔼[𝟙[ωω∗<0]∣ω]]\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\frac{\omega^{2}}{2q_{t}^{\circ}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi q_{t}}}\left[\Delta-\mathbb{E}\left[\mathds{1}[\omega\omega^{\ast}<0]\mid\omega\right]\right] (42)
=e−ω22​qt2​π​qt[Δ−Φ(−mt/qt​|ω|1−mt2/qt).].\displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\frac{\omega^{2}}{2q_{t}}}}{\sqrt{2\pi q_{t}}}\left[\Delta-\Phi\left(\frac{-\nicefrac{{m_{t}}}{{q_{t}}}|\omega|}{\sqrt{1-\nicefrac{{m_{t}^{2}}}{{q_{t}}}}}\right).\right]. (43)

The sign of the derivative is dictated by the term in brackets. If the latter is positive, then the risk increment dℛt/dt\nicefrac{{\differential\mathcal{R}_{t}}}{{\differential t}} is minimal at pt​(ω)=0p_{t}(\omega)=0. If conversely the bracketed term is negative, then the dℛt/dt\nicefrac{{\differential\mathcal{R}_{t}}}{{\differential t}} is minimal for pt​(ω)=1p_{t}(\omega)=1. The myopic policy for the cumulative risk is thus

pℛ,t∘(ω)=𝟙[Φ(−mt/qt​|ω|1−mt2/qt)≥Δ]\displaystyle p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\omega)=\mathds{1}\left[\Phi\left(\frac{-\nicefrac{{m_{t}}}{{q_{t}}}|\omega|}{\sqrt{1-\nicefrac{{m_{t}^{2}}}{{q_{t}}}}}\right)\geq\Delta\right] (44)

If Δ>1/2\Delta>\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}, the optimal rule never makes a query, since even a random classifier that always attempts a prediction will achieve, on average, smaller cost increment. If Δ≤1/2\Delta\leq\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}} on the other hand, pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} reduces to an adaptive margin-based policy of the form

pℛ,t∘(ω)=𝟙[|ω|≤κt∘]\displaystyle p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\omega)=\mathds{1}[|\omega|\leq\kappa^{\circ}_{t}] (45)

with

κt∘=qt∘​2​(qt/mt2−1)​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|.\displaystyle\kappa^{\circ}_{t}=\sqrt{q_{t}^{\circ}}\sqrt{2(\nicefrac{{q_{t}}}{{m_{t}^{2}}}-1)}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|. (46)

This recovers equations 14 of Res. 4.1. The expression of the threshold κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} thus depends on the model weights as time tt, as encapsulated by the summary statistics mt,qtm_{t},q_{t}. When the model is trained with the Adatron rule with η=2\eta=2, and guided at each round by the pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}, an analysis of the ODEs (7) allows to precisely ascertain the asymptotic behavior of κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} in the limit of large training times t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. This is the objective of the following subsection.

Remark C.1.

The 1/t\nicefrac{{1}}{{t}} decay of the threshold plays a key role in ensuring the sub-linear growth of the cumulative cost. One can show along identical lines that if a non-adaptive threshold is used, pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤κ]p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\kappa] with κ\kappa constant in time, one instead observes a linear in time increase

no matter the margin κ>0\kappa>0.

As an additional remark, note that the number of queried samples scales logarithmically with time, as the policy gets more stringent.

𝒬t∘=2π​4​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|ϕ⁡(2​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|)​ln⁡(t)+o⁡(ln⁡(t)).\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{t}^{\circ}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{4\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|}{\phi\left(\sqrt{2}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|\right)}\ln(t)+o(\ln(t)). (69)

(70)

Namely, the myopic policy pℛ,t∘​(⋅)p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t}(\cdot) makes the test error decay exponentially with the number of queries. which concludes the derivation of Remark 4.2.

where the expectation bears over

Appendix D Experimental details

D.1 Benchmarked strategies

We provide additional details on the implementation of the selection policies represented in Figs. 3, 7, which have been proposed in the literature for the problem considered in the present work, namely online active binary classification with a linear classifier trained with Adatron/Perceptron updates Anlauf and Biehl (1989); Rosenblatt (1958). Let us note that all these algorithms exhibit comparable O⁡(d​tF)O(dt_{F}) runtime.

b-sampling

(b-spl) (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004) proposes a margin-based selection rule with (constant-in-time) acquisition probability

pt​(⋅)=bb+|⋅|,\displaystyle p_{t}(\cdot)=\frac{b}{b+|\cdot|}, (77)

for a given choice of bandwidth b>0b>0. As specified in the original work, the Perceptron rule was used to update the model weights, instead of the Adatron rule. For each one of Figs. 3, 7, 8, 9 a grid-search over N=50N=50 values for the parameter bb, evenly spread on a logarithmic grid between 10−2,1010^{-2},10, was performed, and only the trajectory corresponding to the value minimizing the terminal cumulative cost ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} was plotted.

Adaptive b-sampling

(ada-b-spl) (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004) is an adaptive version of b-sampling, which prescribes to increase the bandwidth bb as the square-root of the cumulative number of mistakes on queried samples, namely

pt​(⋅)=β​1+ℳ~tβ1+ℳ~t+|⋅|,\displaystyle p_{t}(\cdot)=\frac{\beta\sqrt{1+\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{t}}}{\beta\sqrt{1+\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{t}}+|\cdot|}, (78)

with

ℳ~t=∑i=1t​dσi𝟙[⟨wi,xi⟩yi<0],\displaystyle\tilde{\mathcal{M}}_{t}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{td}\sigma_{i}\mathds{1}[\left\langle w_{i},x_{i}\right\rangle y_{i}<0]\,, (79)

for a given choice of tunable hyperparameter β>0\beta>0. The value leading to minimal ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} over a logarithmic grid of size 5050 between 10−2,1010^{-2},10 was plotted.

Logistic sampling

(log.-spl) (Sculley, 2007) instead proposes a constant-in-time exponential (rather than sigmoid) ansatz for the acquisition probability

pt(⋅)=e−γ|⋅|,\displaystyle p_{t}(\cdot)=e^{-\gamma|\cdot|}, (80)

with hyperparameter γ>0\gamma>0, again leveraging the Perceptron training rule. The value leading to minimal ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} over a logarithmic grid of size 5050 between 10−2,1010^{-2},10 was plotted.

Active Perceptron

(AL-Perc) (Dasgupta et al., 2005) corresponds to an Adatron rule with learning rate η=2\eta=2, and a hard inner-margin threshold policy

pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤st],\displaystyle p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq s_{t}], (81)

where the threshold sts_{t} is initialized at 1/d\nicefrac{{1}}{{\sqrt{d}}}, and divided by 22 every time a streak of R∈ℕR\in\mathbb{N} consecutive correct predictions is achieved. It thus resembles the myopic policy (15) of Result 4.1, in that it involves a shrinking margin. 5050 values of the patience parameter RR between 11 and 101101 were simulated, and the value leading to minimal terminal cumulative cost plotted. Note that the pseudo-code of the original paper Dasgupta et al. (2005) does not explicitly prescribe to reset the streak count after every threshold-halving, but the subsequent work of Monteleoni and Kaariainen (2007) does. We implement the latter prescription.

Passive baseline

(random) We finally include the baseline of a random selection policy, which queries a sample with constant prediction p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], irrespective of the sample. 5050 values of p∈[0.01,1]p\in[0.01,1] were simulated, and the value minimizing the terminal cost retained and plotted. Updates are performed using the Perceptron rule.

In addition to these classical baselines, we implement the following policies, taking inspiration from the characterization of the myopic policy of Res. 4.1.

Inner-margin with shrinking threshold

(K/t\nicefrac{{K}}{{t}}-inner-margin) corresponds to a inner-margin policy

pt(⋅)=𝟙[|⋅|≤K/t],\displaystyle p_{t}(\cdot)=\mathds{1}[|\cdot|\leq\nicefrac{{K}}{{t}}], (82)

with tunable hyperparameter KK. In Figs. 3, 7, 8, 9, a grid-search over N=50N=50 values for the parameter KK, evenly spread on a logarithmic grid between 10−2,5010^{-2},50, was performed, and only the trajectory corresponding in hindsight to the value minimizing the terminal cumulative cost ℛtF\mathcal{R}_{t_{F}} was plotted.

Inner-margin with theory-prescribed threshold

(K∘/t\nicefrac{{K^{\circ}}}{{t}}-inner-margin) Note that Res. 4.1, Eq. 15 affords a particular prescription for the parameter KK above. The black lines in Figs. 3, 7, 8, 9 correspond to this particular value K=K∘K=K^{\circ}. For instance, for Δ=0.2,q0=0.1,η=2\Delta=0.2,q_{0}=0.1,\eta=2, K∘≈2.52K^{\circ}\approx 2.52. In contrast to all other baselines, this policy is hyperparameter-free, and calls for no tuning.

We note that the inner-margin policy performs comparatively well against all studied baselines in all probed settings, provided the hyperparameter KK is tuned. The particular prescription K∘K^{\circ} (46) on the other hand performs poorly on real datasets, and is found to query too often.

D.2 Preprocessing of the datasets

Covid 19 dataset

(Chowdhury et al., 2020; Rahman et al., 2021) The original dataset includes 36163616 chest X-ray scans from Covid-positive patients, and 1754917549 scans from patients with no infection, non-Covid infection, pneumonia. For simplicity, the latter two classes were discarded, and the class of no infection was downsampled to 36163616 images to balance the dataset, yielding a total of 72327232 samples. Each image was resized to 40×4040\times 40 pixel. A held-out dataset was constituted from 100100 samples, and used to fit the scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) StandardScaler. The latter was then used to transform the remaining n=7132n=7132 images, which corresponds to the total stream length. At each round, the sample is normalized to unit norm before being presented to the model and policy.

Chest-Xray scans dataset

(Kermany et al., 2018) The dataset includes 58635863 chest X-ray scans from patients with(out) pneumonia. The two classes were not balanced. Each image was resized to 40×4040\times 40 pixel. A held-out dataset was constituted from 100100 samples, and used to fit the scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) StandardScaler. The latter was then used to transform the remaining n=5763n=5763 images, which corresponds to the total stream length. At each round, the sample is normalized to unit norm before being presented to the model and policy.

D.3 Training of the 2-layer neural network

We now detail the training procedure followed to obtain the network weights v,Wv,W, from which Fig.  4 was then produced, using the expression of Result 4.4. The readout weights vv were initialized, and kept fixed throughout training, to the all-ones vector v=(1,1)⊤v=(1,1)^{\top}. The weights WW were initialized with i.i.d standard Gaussian entries, then updated n=2000n=2000 times with the online gradient update

Wi+1=Wi−η​ℓ′​(v⊤​g​(Wi​xi+1),sign(⟨β,xi+1⟩))​(v⊙g′​(Wi​xi+1))​xi+1⊤\displaystyle W_{i+1}=W_{i}-\eta\ell^{\prime}\left(v^{\top}g(W_{i}x_{i+1}),\sgn(\left\langle\beta,x_{i+1}\right\rangle)\right)(v\odot g^{\prime}(W_{i}x_{i+1}))x_{i+1}^{\top} (83)

with unit learning rate η=1\eta=1, on the logistic loss ℓ⁡(z,y)=ln⁡(1+exp⁡(−y​z))\ell(z,y)=\ln(1+\exp{-yz}), and without any data selection. The activation g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) was taken to be GeLU. Simulations were conducted in dimension d=500d=500.

Appendix E Logistic loss

The main text focuses on the Adatron online training procedure (Anlauf and Biehl, 1989; Engel and van den Broeck, 2001), which can be viewed as a variant of the classical Perceptron rule (Rosenblatt, 1958). While these losses are classically considered in many works on online active classification (Dasgupta, 2004; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2004; Sculley, 2007; Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2009), losses such as the logistic loss are more commonly leveraged in day-to-day machine learning practice. The present Appendix is devoted to expanding the discussion of the main text the latter, highlighting in particular the difference with Adatron/Perceptron rules. In fact, the use of the logistic loss in the SGD updates (1) instead of the Adatron/Perceptron loss leads to a quantitatively different behavior, notably in terms of growth rates of the cumulative cost. This is the object of the present Appendix.

E.1 Myopic policy for the cumulative cost

We revisit the analysis of the myopic rule pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} for the cumulative cost (4), characterized for the Adatron rule in Result 4.1, for the case of the logistic loss. While pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} still takes the form (13), since the latter only depend on the loss through the current-time summary statistics values mt∘,qtm_{t}^{\circ},q_{t}, the asymptotic behavior of the threshold κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} differs. The following conjecture surmises that the latter tends to a non-zero limit in the large-time limit t→∞t\rightarrow\infty, as opposed to the 1/t\nicefrac{{1}}{{t}} decay for Adatron.

Conjecture E.1 (Myopic policy for the cumulative cost, logistic loss).

Let ℓ\ell be the logistic loss ℓ⁡(z)=ln⁡(1+exp⁡(−z))\ell(z)=\ln(1+\exp{-z}). If the equation

∫u=0∞∫v=−2​z​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|−uz2​z​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|−uze−v222​π[ℓ′(u+zv)(2zv−ηℓ′(u+zv)))]dudv=0\displaystyle\int\limits_{u=0}^{\infty}\int\limits_{v=\frac{-\sqrt{2}z\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|-u}{z}}^{\frac{\sqrt{2}z\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|-u}{z}}\frac{e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}}}{2\pi}\left[\ell^{\prime}(u+zv)\left(2zv-\eta\ell^{\prime}(u+zv))\right)\right]\differential u\differential v=0 (84)

admits a positive solution z∗>0z^{\ast}>0, then the threshold κt∘\kappa^{\circ}_{t} (46) admits a non-zero limit

κt∘→t→∞2​z∗​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|.\displaystyle\kappa^{\circ}_{t}\xrightarrow{t\rightarrow\infty}\sqrt{2}z^{\ast}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|. (85)

Furthermore, when the policy pℛ,t∘p^{\circ}_{\mathcal{R},t} is employed, the test error decays asymptotically as

εg,t∘=z∗/π(−3η[∫u=0∞∫v=−2​z∗​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|−uz∗2​z∗​|erf−1​(2​Δ−1)|−uz∗e−v222​π[ℓ′(u+z∗v)(2(u+z∗v)−ηℓ′(u+z∗v)))]dudv])13​t−13+o⁡(t−13)\displaystyle\varepsilon_{g,t}^{\circ}=\frac{\nicefrac{{z^{\ast}}}{{\pi}}}{\left(-3\eta\left[\int\limits_{u=0}^{\infty}\int\limits_{v=\frac{-\sqrt{2}z^{\ast}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|-u}{z^{\ast}}}^{\frac{\sqrt{2}z^{\ast}\left|\mathrm{erf}^{-1}\left(2\Delta-1\right)\right|-u}{z^{\ast}}}\frac{e^{-\frac{v^{2}}{2}}}{2\pi}\left[\ell^{\prime}(u+z^{\ast}v)\left(2(u+z^{\ast}v)-\eta\ell^{\prime}(u+z^{\ast}v))\right)\right]\differential u\differential v\right]\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}}t^{-\frac{1}{3}}+o(t^{-\frac{1}{3}}) (86)

As will be detailed in the following subsection, Eq. (84) is in fact a necessary condition for the following two asymptotic statements to be self-consistent. Heuristically, we numerically observe the predicted scaling and leading asymptotic term across a broad range of values for Δ,η\Delta,\eta (see Fig. 10), leading us to surmise that Conj. E.1 holds more broadly.

An immediate corollary of Conj. E.1 is that although the cumulative cost (4), number of mistakes (5) and number of queries (3) still admit sub-linear growth, the latter is no longer logarithmic, but power-law.

Remark E.2 (Cumulative cost scaling).

The cumulative cost ℛt∘\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t}, number of mistakes ℳt∘\mathcal{M}^{\circ}_{t}, and number of queries 𝒬t∘\mathcal{Q}^{\circ}_{t} scale as ℛt∘,ℳt∘,𝒬t∘≍t2/3\mathcal{R}^{\circ}_{t},\mathcal{M}^{\circ}_{t},\mathcal{Q}^{\circ}_{t}\asymp t^{\nicefrac{{2}}{{3}}}.

This power-law is to be contrasted to the much milder logarithmic growth induced by the Adatron loss, as summarized in Rem. 4.2.
